solution:
India has five physiographic divisions: the Himalayas, the North Indian Plains, the Peninsula, the Coastal Plains and the Island groups. Brazil has four: the Highlands, the Great Escarpment, the Coasts and the Plains.

Mountains: India has the Himalayas, one of the young fold mountain systems of the world, running from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh in several parallel ranges. Brazil has no very high or long extending mountains at all — a large part of it is occupied by highlands, plateaus and small mountains.

Plains: India's North Indian Plains are extensive, stretching from Rajasthan and Punjab in the west to Assam in the east between the Himalayas and the Peninsula. In Brazil wide plains are confined to two areas only, the Amazon basin in the north and the Paraguay-Parana source region in the south-west, and even the coastal plains are restricted in their expanse.

Plateaus: India's Peninsula lies south of the plains and tapers towards the Indian Ocean, holding many plateaus and hill ranges with the Aravalis, the oldest fold mountains here, in the north. Brazil's Brazilian and Guyana Highlands are the core of the South American continent and slope gradually towards the north.

Coasts: India's coastline of about 7500 km lies on the west and east of the Peninsula and the two coasts differ sharply. Brazil's coastline of about 7400 km divides into a northern and an eastern coast, both on the Atlantic.

Brazil also has one division India does not — the Great Escarpment, which demarcates the eastern side of the Highlands.

[Note: this chapter describes the drainage of India and Brazil but does not state what measures are being taken to control pollution in the rivers of India, so the points below are not taken from it.]

The measures ordinarily taken are of three kinds. Untreated sewage and industrial effluent are the main source of the pollution, so towns and industries along a river are required to treat their waste water before releasing it and effluent treatment plants are set up for the purpose. Government programmes have been undertaken to clean particular rivers, the Ganga among them, by building treatment capacity along their banks and cleaning the river channel itself. And the practices that pollute a river directly — dumping refuse and idols into it, washing and bathing at the ghats, and the run-off of fertilisers and pesticides from the fields — are discouraged through law and through public awareness.

The chapter does supply the reason such measures matter most here: the Ganga plains are fertile and densely settled, so a very large number of people depend on that river directly.

The North Indian Plains lie between the Himalaya Mountains in the north and the Peninsula in the south, and extend from Rajasthan and Punjab in the west to Assam in the east. They are mostly a flat, low-lying area.

The plains are divided into two parts. The part lying to the east of the Aravalis is the basin of the river Ganga and is therefore known as the Ganga Plains; it slopes eastward. Most of the West Bengal State of India and Bangladesh together form the delta of the Ganga-Brahmaputra system, known as the Sunderbans, which is considered to be the world's largest delta.

The western part of the plains is occupied by desert, known as the Thar Desert or Marusthali, which covers most of Rajasthan. To the north of the desert lie the plains of Punjab, spread to the west of the Aravalis and the Delhi ranges. These plains were formed by the depositional work of the river Sutluj and its tributaries and slope towards the west. Because the soil here is very fertile, agriculture is largely practised in this region.

Pantanal is one of the largest wetlands in the world. It lies towards the south-west part of the highland areas, in north-western Mato Grosso do Sul in Brazil, and extends into Argentina too.

The reasons for the swamps there follow from where it lies. It is part of the plains that form the source region of the Paraguay and Parana rivers, so a large amount of water collects in it from the surrounding highlands. The land itself is a low, wide plain: the source region of the Paraguay slopes towards the south and that of the Parana towards the south-west, and both are gentle slopes, so the water that gathers there cannot drain away quickly.

Water that arrives faster than it can leave stands on the surface, and a region of swamps and marshes is the result.

[Note: the chapter states where Pantanal is and what it is, but does not itself set out the reasons for the swamps, so the explanation above is drawn from what it says about the slope and drainage of that region.]

A water divide is high ground that separates two drainage basins, sending the rivers on either side of it in different directions.

The Western Ghats form a major water divide in the Peninsula. The peninsular rivers are divided by them into east-flowing rivers, which meet the Bay of Bengal, and west-flowing rivers, which meet the Arabian Sea. The rivers rising on the western slope are short and swift and form estuaries rather than deltas, while the long east-flowing rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri cross the whole peninsula.

The Aravali ranges act as a water divide in the north-west: the land to their east drains into the Ganga basin through tributaries such as the Chambal and the Banas, while the region to their west is the desert and the Punjab plains built by the Sutluj.

The Vindhyas act as a water divide in central India, separating the basins on either side of them.

The Himalayas are the great divide of the north, and the Himalayan rivers — the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra systems — rise beyond and within them.

The Amazon collects its headwaters from the eastern slopes of the Andes Mountains in Peru. Its basin forms the largest plain land of Brazil and lies between the Guyana Highlands and the Brazilian Highlands, in the northern part of the country, sloping eastwards.

The basin is about 1300 km wide in the west and narrows eastward; its width is least, about 240 km, where the Guyana and Brazilian Highlands come closer, and it widens again as the river approaches the Atlantic Ocean. These are mostly forested areas, largely inaccessible because of frequent flooding and dense undergrowth, and most of the Amazon plains are covered by tropical rainforests.

The river receives a huge discharge, about 2 lakh cubic metres per second. As a result it washes off the load supplied to it from the catchment, so sediments are not deposited even at the mouth and the dense network of distributaries typical of a river mouth is by and large absent. Instead a series of islands has developed along the mouth, beyond the coastline and into the Atlantic Ocean. At its mouth the Amazon channel is 150 km wide, and most of the river's course is suitable for navigation.

The Himalayas is one of the young fold mountains in the world and a major mountain system of the Asian continent. It extends from the Pamir Knot in Tajikistan to the east, and in India it runs from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh.

It is not a single mountain range but a system of many parallel ranges. From south to north these are the Siwaliks, the Lesser Himalayas, the Greater Himalayas (Himadri) and the Trans Himalayan ranges. The southernmost, the Siwaliks, is also the youngest, and the ranges are young to old respectively in that order.

The system is also divided from west to east into the Western Himalayas (or Kashmir Himalayas), the Central Himalayas (or Kumaun Himalayas) and the Eastern Himalayas (or Assam Himalayas).

The Himalayas form the northern boundary of the North Indian Plains, which lie between them and the Peninsula.

Brazil has a coastline of about 7400 km, which may be divided into two parts, the northern coast and the eastern coast.

The northern coast extends from Amapa province in the north to Rio Grande do Norte in the east and can be called the North Atlantic coast. It is characterised by the mouths of many rivers, including the Amazon, and is therefore a low-lying region. On it lie Marajo island and the Marajo and Sao Marcos Bays; Marajo is a large coastal island lying between the mouths of the River Amazon and the River Tocantins.

From Rio Grande do Norte the eastern coast extends towards the south. It receives a large number of smaller rivers, and the only major river meeting the Atlantic Ocean here is the Sao Francisco.

The Brazilian coast as a whole is characterised by a large number of beaches and sand dune complexes, and in some areas it is protected by coral reefs and atoll islands.

The area lying to the south of the North Indian Plains and tapering towards the Indian Ocean is called the Indian Peninsula.

It consists of many plateaus and hill ranges. The Aravalis in the north are the oldest fold mountains here. It includes a series of plateaus bordering the Plains, the Vindhya and Satpuda ranges in the central part, and the hilly regions of the Western and Eastern Ghats.

The Western Ghats form a major water divide in the Peninsula, separating the short, swift west-flowing rivers that meet the Arabian Sea from the long east-flowing rivers that meet the Bay of Bengal. The peninsular rivers are rain fed, so they are seasonal in nature and seldom face the problem of floods.

The Great Escarpment is one of Brazil's physiographic divisions. Though it occupies a very small area, the nature of its slope and the effect it has on the climate make it a separate physiographic region.

It demarcates the eastern side of the Highlands. In this region the altitude of the escarpment is 790 m, and in some regions its height decreases gradually. It is very steep particularly from Sao Paulo to Porto Alegre.

Its effect on climate is the reason it matters. The escarpment acts as a barrier to the South-east Trade winds, which gives rise to a rain-shadow area in the north-eastern part of the highlands. The region to the north of this area is called the 'Drought Quadrilateral'.

The direction in which a river flows is decided by the slope of the land, and in Brazil that slope runs away from the west.

The Brazilian Highlands, which occupy a large part of the country, slope gradually towards the north, and a number of rivers take off from the terminal portion of the highlands and flow northwards to meet the Atlantic Ocean; the tributaries of the Amazon flowing through this region make rapids and waterfalls. The Amazon plains themselves slope eastwards. The rivers rising on the southern slopes of the highlands — the Uruguay, Paraguay and Parana — flow south and enter Argentina.

Brazil's coast, moreover, is entirely on the east and north, on the Atlantic Ocean, and its western boundary is inland, shared with other countries. A river flowing west would have nowhere in Brazil to reach the sea. So the rivers of Brazil flow north, east and south, and there are no west-flowing rivers.

The two coasts of India were formed in different ways, and that is what makes them unlike each other.

The western coast borders the Arabian Sea. It is by and large a rocky coast; at places spurs taking off from the Western Ghats extend right up to the coast, and its width is also less. The rivers rising in the Western Ghats have only a short distance to run and are swift, so they form estuaries and not deltas.

The eastern coast borders the Bay of Bengal and has been formed by the depositional work of rivers. Many east-flowing rivers rising in the Western and Eastern Ghats reach this coast. Because the slope of the land is gentle, they flow at lower velocities and deposit the sediment they carry at the coast, so deltas are found along this coast and the coastal plain is wider.

A natural port needs deep water close to the shore and a sheltered, rocky coast.

The eastern coast of India has been formed by the depositional work of rivers. The many east-flowing rivers that reach it flow at lower velocities because of the gentle slope of the land, and deposit the sediment they bring at the coast, so deltas are found all along it. Deposition of this kind keeps the water near the shore shallow and keeps filling up any inlet that might serve as a harbour.

The western coast is the opposite: it is by and large a rocky coast, with spurs from the Western Ghats extending right up to the sea and rivers that form estuaries rather than deltas, so the water there stays deep near the shore.

That is why there are fewer natural ports on the eastern coast of India than on the western one.

The difference lies in how many people live along the two rivers and how they use them.

The Amazon basin is mostly forested and is largely inaccessible because of frequent flooding and dense undergrowth, and most of the Amazon plains are covered by tropical rainforests. Few people live there, so few depend on the river directly.

The Ganga is quite different. Its basin forms the Ganga Plains, a flat low-lying area of fertile soil in which agriculture is largely practised, and it runs through the most closely settled part of India, ending in the Sunderbans, the world's largest delta. Its water is used for drinking, for farming and for daily needs by a very large number of people all along its course.

Because so many people depend on it, pollution in the Ganga reaches human beings directly and at once, whereas the same pollution in the Amazon would pass through a region where almost nobody lives. That is why pollution in the Ganga will affect human life far more greatly.

Group (ii) is correct: Guyana Highlands - Amazon river basin - Brazilan Highlands.

Going from the north-west of Brazil towards the south-east, the Guyana Highlands come first in the far north; then the Amazon river basin, which the chapter says lies between the two highlands and forms the largest plain land of Brazil; and then the Brazilian Highlands, which occupy the south and east of the country.

Group (i) is wrong because the Parana river basin is in the south-west, not the north-west, and it puts the Guyana Highlands after it. Group (iii) is wrong because the Coastal Plains of Brazil lie along the north and east of the country, not in the north-west, and the chapter says they are restricted in their expanse.

Group (i) is correct: Juruika - Xingu - Aragua.

The chapter says that the Brazilian Highlands gradually slope towards the north, that the tributaries of the Amazon flowing through this region make rapids and waterfalls, and that a number of rivers take off from the terminal portion of the highlands and flow northwards to meet the Atlantic Ocean. These three rivers rise in those highlands, south of the Amazon, and so flow northwards into it.

The rivers of group (ii) rise to the north of the Amazon, in the Guyana Highlands, so they flow southwards to join it, and those of group (iii) rise in the west and flow eastwards down the slope of the Amazon plains, which the chapter says slope eastwards.

Group (i) is correct: Karnataka - Maharashtra - Bundelkhand.

Read off figure 3.1, the Karnataka Plateau lies furthest south at about 14° N, the Maharashtra Plateau next at about 19° N, and Bundelkhand furthest north at about 25° N, so the three are named in order from south to north.

Group (ii) is not in order: the Chhota Nagpur Plateau and the Malwa Plateau lie at about the same latitude, so naming Chhota Nagpur first does not put them south to north.

[Note: group (iii), Telangana - Maharashtra - Marwad, also names three plateaus in order from south to north on that map — about 17° N, 19° N and 26° N — so as printed this question admits two correct answers. Group (i) is given here as the answer because its three plateaus lie one above the other in a single line northwards, whereas the Marwad Plateau lies away to the north-west, beyond the Aravalis.]
